title: Case: Adyen, the Single Platform With a Banking Licence

know: The history in dated steps: founded in Amsterdam in 2006; a European acquiring license, which its history page dates only to the period 2006 to 2012; banking license 2017; listing on Euronext Amsterdam in June 2018; US federal branch 2021; embedded financial products March 2022; UK banking authorization September 2023; the 2023 margin fall (55% in 2022 to 46% in 2023) and recovery (50% in 2024, 53% in 2025); Talon.One and Orb announced in April and June 2026 and closed on 1 July 2026.

The single-platform bet in Adyen's own words (2025 annual report): operate 'the essential layers of the financial stack ourselves', 'a single platform built entirely in-house', licenses held to work 'without relying on partner banks', with data centers as the main capital expenditure (5% of net revenue in 2025, 7% expected for 2026).

The figures with their definitions: processed volume, net revenue (what Adyen keeps after passing on interchange and scheme fees), EBITDA margin, take rate (17.0 basis points in 2025), full-stack share (84%), in-person volume (€310.9 billion, 22% of volume), the three pillars (Digital, Unified Commerce, Platforms), top ten merchants at 11% of revenue.

Where the single platform stops by Adyen's own disclosures (16% of volume not full-stack, banking partners named as a concentration risk in locations where it has no acquiring license, Orb described in June 2026 as run as an 'incubator' that keeps serving other providers, 'convergence' stated as intent with no date) and where the public record stops (the cities, operators and number of its data centers beyond six named regions, the identity of the single large-volume customer, what has been integrated of the acquired products).
believe: 'Single platform, built in-house' is a dated description of Adyen's payments and banking core, accurate there, and no longer a description of the whole company.

Owning the regulated layer is a choice with a visible price (capital, supervision, capital expenditure) and a visible return in Adyen's accounts; it is not available to, or sensible for, most builders.
can_do: State which Adyen products run on the platform it built and which were bought in 2026, and what Adyen has and has not said about integrating them.
Read Adyen's volume, net revenue, margin and take rate together and explain a year in which they move in different directions.
Name the practices in Adyen's record that a builder can adopt and the assets it cannot.

audience.who: Engineers and architects new to payments who have read the Stripe case and the mechanism chapters of Parts I to VIII, and who integrate with Adyen, evaluate it, or are tempted to copy it.
already_knows: What an API, a webhook, a ledger, sharding and a data center are.
From earlier chapters: acquirer, issuer, interchange, settlement, payout, safeguarding, payment facilitator; they are glossed again in one clause where first used here.
Stripe's order of construction from the previous chapter: interface first, regulated layer assembled afterward.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given the claim that everything bought from Adyen is one platform, the reader answers as of November 2026 with the dated facts and the stated limits.
acceptance_criteria.probe: An architect at a retailer says in November 2026: 'Adyen builds everything itself on one platform, so whatever we buy from them is one integration with one set of reports.' Using only this chapter: is that right?
acceptance_criteria.expected: For payments, acquiring, terminals and the banking products it is what Adyen states: 'a single platform built entirely in-house' on its own licenses (annual report 2025). It is no longer true of everything Adyen sells: on 1 July 2026 Adyen closed the purchases of Talon.One (loyalty and promotions, €750 million) and Orb (usage billing, $335 million). Adyen says Talon.One's engine is being integrated into its architecture; in June 2026 it said that Orb runs under 'an incubator model', keeps 'supporting multi-PSP environments', and that 'the strategic intent is convergence', with no date; on 28 October 2026 it wrote of 'the successful ongoing integration of Talon.One and Orb' without saying what has been joined. Until then a customer using those products should expect separate systems and ask Adyen what is shared. No Adyen document says it has abandoned building in-house; a 9 April 2026 release still contrasted Adyen with providers that rely on 'acquired technologies'.

acceptance_criteria.statement: Given Adyen's 2025 figures moving in different directions, the reader explains them from the definitions and from what Adyen reports.
acceptance_criteria.probe: In 2025 Adyen's processed volume grew 8% and its net revenue grew 18%. A colleague concludes that Adyen raised its prices. Using only this chapter: what does Adyen's own reporting say?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Processed volume grew 8% as reported and 21% excluding a single large-volume customer that Adyen does not name; net revenue, which is what Adyen keeps after passing on interchange and scheme fees, grew 18%. The take rate (net revenue divided by processed volume) rose from 15.5 to 17.0 basis points, which Adyen attributes to 'changes in the overall merchant mix', not to price increases. Adyen prices in volume tiers, so less volume from a very large customer lowers volume more than revenue. In the first half of 2026 the take rate was 16.2 basis points, which Adyen attributes to 'expected volume tiering'.

acceptance_criteria.statement: The reader separates what a builder can adopt from Adyen's record from the assets that cannot be copied, and names the limit Adyen itself discloses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: A logistics platform with a payments team of nine reads this chapter and wants 'what Adyen has'. Using only this chapter: what can it adopt, what can it not, and what does Adyen say about how its own largest customers buy?
acceptance_criteria.expected: Adopt: one accounting core for every money movement with entries that must sum to zero, checked when written (Adyen's 2021 account, five years old); one place where each improvement takes effect for all customers; API versions visible in every request. Cannot copy: banking licenses in three jurisdictions, data-center capacity bought with 5 to 7% of net revenue, an estate of 878,000 transacting terminals. Adyen's own risk section says large enterprise merchants typically work with several payment providers and may shift volume, so even its customers do not treat one platform as the only one.

acceptance_criteria.statement: A reader of the introduction alone can predict the chapter's sections and the kind of evidence it uses.
acceptance_criteria.probe: After reading only the introduction: what will this chapter establish about Adyen, in what order, and from what kinds of source?
acceptance_criteria.expected: How to read the case; history by date; the single-platform bet in Adyen's words; licenses and what they allow; unified commerce and terminals; platforms and financial products; the 2026 acquisitions and what they change; figures with definitions; the documented engineering record and its age; what transfers; where the evidence stops. Sources: the audited annual report, shareholder letters and business updates, press releases, license and documentation pages, engineering posts, each dated.

thesis.question: What does Adyen's dated public record show about building payments as one platform under its own banking license, and which of its practices can a builder use?
thesis.claim: Adyen's record shows a company that chose to operate the regulated layers itself for enterprise customers (one platform built in-house, its own acquiring and banking licenses in the EU, the US and the UK, its own data-center capacity) and that reports its volume, net revenue and margin in audited figures; Adyen itself discloses where the single platform stops (16% of 2025 volume was not full-stack, and it names banking partners in locations where it has no acquiring license), and since 1 July 2026 the phrase describes Adyen's payments and banking core and not the whole company, because loyalty and usage billing were bought and Adyen describes one of them, Orb, as run under 'an incubator model'. A builder can adopt the practice of one accounting core and one place for every change; the licenses, the data centers and the terminal estate are assets built over two decades, not a design a builder can adopt.
thesis.disputed_by: The view that Adyen proves building everything in-house on one platform is the correct architecture for payments, that the company still builds and does not buy, and that the 2026 acquisitions are a footnote; or the opposite view, that the acquisitions show the single platform was always a slogan.
thesis.so_what: A customer integrating Adyen before July 2026 touched one platform; one that adds Orb or Talon.One should ask what is shared (credentials, events, reports) and plan for separate systems until Adyen says otherwise. A builder notes that Adyen attributes its 53% margin to the single platform, that the attribution is Adyen's own, and that the platform and licenses behind it took from 2006 to 2023 to assemble; the margin is not evidence for a design a team could reproduce in a year.
thesis.how_why: The annual report for 2025 states the choice as a sequence: first 'our single global platform', so that an improvement 'takes effect everywhere, without reintegration work'; then 'our own banking licenses in the EU, US, and UK', to work 'without relying on partner banks'; data centers are the main capital expenditure. Adyen credits the platform for its margin ('the underlying operational efficiency inherent to our single-platform architecture', H1 2026), which is its own attribution, not an independent finding. The same documents mark the edges: 84% of 2025 volume was full-stack; concentration risk sits 'at banking partners in locations where there are no own direct acquiring licenses'; Orb is preserved under 'an incubator model' and keeps 'supporting multi-PSP environments'. In August 2026 Adyen wrote 'we are no longer just a payments company'. Its 2021 engineering account describes one accounting framework whose entries must sum to zero when written, which is the practice a builder can take. Its posts on the platform's architecture are mostly from 2018 to 2021, with later ones on partitioning (2023 to 2025) and one of 2026 that adds scale, so the chapter's account of internals is short and dated; the cities and operators of its data centers (it names six regions), what has been integrated of the acquisitions and the identity of the single large-volume customer behind its 2025 volume figures are not public.

supporting_claims.claim: Adyen's dated history is an order of construction: an acquiring license and enterprise merchants first, the banking permissions next (EU 2017, US 2021, UK 2023), financial products on those permissions from 2022, and adjacent software last and by purchase in 2026.

The single-platform bet is stated by Adyen as a sequence (one platform, its own licenses, its own infrastructure) and has a visible price in capital expenditure and supervision; an integrator meets it as specific documented behavior (terminals and online payments on one platform, payouts paid ahead of network settlement, one accounting core), not as a single API.

Adyen itself discloses where the platform stops: 16% of 2025 volume was not full-stack, it names banking partners, as a concentration risk, in locations where it has no acquiring license (that they stand in for Adyen there is the author's inference), it sold no billing engine, tax engine or merchant-of-record service of its own, and since 1 July 2026 two bought products sit beside the platform, one of them described in June 2026 as run under an incubator model.

Adyen's audited figures have to be read with their definitions and together: volume, net revenue, take rate and margin moved in different directions in 2025 because of merchant mix and tiered pricing, and the link from the single platform to the margin is Adyen's own attribution.

The engineering record is thin and its architecture posts are mostly from 2018 to 2021; what a builder can take from it is practice (one accounting core checked when written, one place for each change, versions visible in every request), while the licenses, the data centers and the terminal estate are assets, and several questions have no public answer.

role.contribution: Supplies the second company's record, including Adyen's own statements of where its platform and licenses stop and the 2026 acquisitions, so that the comparison does not set Stripe's documents against Adyen's slogan.

additional_patterns.applies_to: history and acquisitions: dated steps in order, 2006 to 2023 and April to October 2026
bet, licenses, in-person, platforms: the bet as a whole, then each layer and product line it produced

flow.rationale: The reader first learns how company evidence is weighed, then gets the history, because the thesis is about an order of construction and every later section refers to a date in it. The bet is quoted before the layers it names (licenses, in-person, platform products), so that each layer is read as a consequence and each ends on the edge Adyen discloses. The acquisitions follow the product edge they cross. The figures come after the acquisitions because the 2026 guidance, headcount and capital expenditure cannot be read without them; putting the figures first would present a 53% margin before the reader knows what the platform is or what changed in July. The engineering record comes late because it is the thinnest and oldest evidence and feeds directly into what transfers; the list of what is not public closes the body so that nothing after it is mistaken for fact.

hook.content: In November 2026 an architect at a retailer says: 'Adyen builds everything itself on one platform, so whatever we buy from them is one integration with one set of reports.' On 9 April 2026 an Adyen press release said almost the same: 'Unlike many providers that rely on a patchwork of acquired technologies and third-party integrations, Adyen has built its entire financial technology stack on a single platform.' On 1 July 2026 Adyen closed the purchase of two software companies.

bridge.from_reader_world: An engineer who has just read how Stripe started from an interface and added the regulated layer afterward expects the second company to be the tidy opposite: one platform, one bank, built in-house, end of story.
bridge.to_topic: Adyen's own documents confirm that picture for payments and banking, mark its edges themselves, and since July 2026 no longer describe the whole company; the case reads those documents by date.

thesis_statement.text: Adyen chose to operate the regulated layers itself for enterprise customers and reports the result in audited figures; it discloses where the single platform stops, and since 1 July 2026 the phrase describes its payments and banking core, not the whole company. A builder can adopt its practices of one accounting core and one place for every change, not its licenses, data centers or terminal estate.

evidence.what: Adyen press release of 9 April 2026 (Intelligent Money Movement): 'Unlike many providers that rely on a patchwork of acquired technologies and third-party integrations, Adyen has built its entire financial technology stack on a single platform.' https://www.adyen.com/press-and-media/adyen-launches-intelligent-money-movement
evidence.shows: The architect's sentence in the hook repeats what Adyen itself said seven months earlier.

evidence.what: Adyen's closing release of 1 July 2026: 'Both transactions officially closed on July 1, 2026' (Talon.One and Orb). https://www.adyen.com/press-and-media/adyen-closes-talonone-and-orb-acquisitions-announces-leadership-updates
evidence.shows: The sentence acquired a date on which it stopped covering everything Adyen sells.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adyen operates the regulated layers itself on one platform for enterprise customers and reports audited figures; it marks the edges of that platform itself; since July 2026 the single platform is its payments and banking core, not the company; and what transfers to a builder is practice, not assets.

sections.heading: How to Read This Case
sections.controlling_idea: Every statement about Adyen is labeled documented, widely reported or inferred and carries its date; the sources differ in weight, and some could not be reached.

advances_thesis.how: Sets the rules of evidence the rest of the case is held to, including the flag on engineering sources older than three years.

transition_in.introduces: The rules for reading company evidence.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Claims are documented, widely reported or labeled inference; the research cut-off is 17 November 2026; and the sources rank from the audited annual report through unaudited letters and updates, press releases and undated license and documentation pages to engineering posts, most of them from 2018 to 2021 and flagged with their age.

evidence.what: The source set: Annual Report 2025 (audited, signed 5 March 2026); H2 2025 and H1 2026 shareholder letters and the Q3 2026 business update (unaudited); press releases 2018 to 2026; adyen.com license, pricing and about pages and docs.adyen.com (n.d., accessed November 2026); knowledge-hub engineering posts 2018 to 2026.
evidence.shows: Tells the reader which kind of statement each later sentence rests on.
evidence.source: brief-companies-and-bets 'How to read this brief'; brief-reliability-and-scale 0.2

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Five things could not be reached or confirmed and are either left out or marked: the official filing of the annual report, the earnings calls, the 2023 Investor Day targets and share-price fall, the full status-page history, and any Adyen statement that the 2026 deals were its first acquisitions.

evidence.what: Research limitations recorded in the briefs: the annual report was read from a copy of the printed version (not the official ESEF filing); the calls of 23 April, 11 June and 13 August 2026 were not transcribed; the 2023 Investor Day targets and the August 2023 share-price fall were recalled, not fetched; status.adyen.com history is truncated to three items a month. Adyen's history page (n.d., accessed November 2026) lists no acquisition before Orb and Talon.One.
evidence.shows: Marks the boundary of the sources before any claim is built on them.
evidence.source: brief-companies-and-bets and brief-reliability-and-scale, 'Research limitation'; https://www.adyen.com/about re-fetched

transition_in.introduces: What could not be read, and how the chapter treats it.

sections.heading: From an Acquiring License to Three Banking Permissions: 2006 to 2023
sections.controlling_idea: Adyen's dated steps run from an acquiring license and enterprise merchants, through a banking license in 2017 and a listing in 2018, to a US branch, financial products and a UK authorization, with one visible stumble in 2023.

advances_thesis.how: Supplies the dated sequence that the thesis calls an order of construction.

transition_in.introduces: The first body of evidence: the history, by date.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adyen was founded in Amsterdam in 2006 and its own history lists a European acquiring license, point-of-sale and risk tools among the steps of 2006 to 2012, for a customer it describes as the enterprise.

evidence.what: https://www.adyen.com/about (n.d., accessed November 2026): 'We were founded in Amsterdam in 2006. We secured a European acquiring license, added POS and risk tools, and expanded into San Francisco, London, Paris, and Stockholm' (period 2006 to 2012); 'Built for enterprise, not adapted to it.'
evidence.shows: The regulated permission and the large merchant come first in Adyen's own account; the page does not date the license within the period.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Between 2016 and 2020 Adyen became a bank and a listed company: a European banking license in 2017, acquiring licenses in Asia-Pacific, a listing on Euronext Amsterdam in June 2018 at €240 a share, and a long-term contract with eBay signed the same year.

evidence.what: US branch release of 14 June 2021: 'its European banking license (obtained in 2017)'. IPO release of 11 June 2018: offer price €240, 'implying a market capitalization of €7.1 billion', existing shares only; trading from 13 June 2018. Annual Report 2025, note on the long-term contract: 'In 2018 Adyen entered into a long-term contract with eBay'. About page: 2016 to 2020, 'added acquiring licenses across APAC, including Singapore, Hong Kong, Australia, New Zealand, and Malaysia'.
evidence.shows: Dates the move from licensed acquirer to bank and to public reporting, which is why audited figures exist from 2018.

transition_in.introduces: The second period, 2016 to 2020: the bank and the listing.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: From 2021 to 2023 the banking permission was extended to the United States and the United Kingdom, and in between, in March 2022, Adyen announced accounts, cards and capital built on it; a table gives all the steps to 2026.

evidence.what: OCC approval of a Federal Foreign Branch in San Francisco announced 14 June 2021 (Federal Reserve approval 24 May 2021); 'Adyen expands beyond payments, announces embedded financial products', 31 March 2022, with Thom Ruiter's 'without the barriers of regulatory complexity, lengthy product development, or sponsor bank restrictions'; UK banking authorization under Part 4A of FSMA 2000 announced 7 September 2023.
evidence.shows: The license comes before the product in each case: the financial products are announced after the first two permissions exist.

evidence.what: Dated steps 2006 to October 2026: Date | Step | Source and age.
evidence.shows: Lets the reader check the order of construction at a glance.

transition_in.introduces: The third period: the permission extended and products built on it.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The one visible stumble is 2023, when hiring took the EBITDA margin (earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortization as a share of net revenue, both glossed here in a clause and defined in the figures section) from 55% in 2022 to 46%, and the recovery to 50% in 2024 and 53% in 2025 is in the audited accounts.

evidence.what: H1 2023 release (17 August 2023): EBITDA margin 43%, 'primarily impacted by increased wages and salaries stemming from Adyen's investments into scaling its global team'. H2 2023 release (8 February 2024): 'EBITDA margin was 46% for the full year, compared to 55% in 2022'. Annual Report 2025: 53% (2024: 50%).
evidence.shows: Shows that the margin moves with headcount decisions, a fact the figures section needs.

evidence.what: INFERENCE block: the sequence is license, platform breadth, bank, products on the bank; each permission precedes the product that needs it.
evidence.shows: The author's reading of the order, labeled as inference.

transition_in.introduces: The year the run was interrupted, and what the accounts show.

flow.rationale: Dated steps in the order they happened, so the reader sees which permission preceded which product.

sections.heading: The Single-Platform Bet in Adyen's Own Words
sections.controlling_idea: Adyen states its bet as a sequence (platform, licenses, own infrastructure); for an integrator it is an operating claim, not one API, and its price is visible as capital expenditure on data centers.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the bet in quotation, separates the operating claim from the interface the integrator meets, and shows the cost.

transition_in.carries_over: The order in which Adyen built.
transition_in.introduces: The reason Adyen gives for building in that order.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The 2025 annual report states the bet as a strategic choice made 'from the beginning' and carried out in steps: first one global platform, then its own banking licenses, all run on its own infrastructure.

evidence.what: Adyen Annual Report 2025 (signed 5 March 2026; audited), 'The evolution of our foundation': 'rather than build a business around the limitations of external providers, we would develop and operate the essential layers of the financial stack ourselves'; 'The first step was our single global platform'; an improvement 'takes effect everywhere, without reintegration work'; 'acquiring our own banking licenses in the EU, US, and UK ... without relying on partner banks, improving reliability and settlement speed'. 'Adyen at a glance': 'a single platform built entirely in-house ... all operated end-to-end on our own infrastructure and banking licenses'.
evidence.shows: The claim is Adyen's own, dated February to March 2026, and names three layers.
evidence.source: brief-companies-and-bets 2.2; quotes re-checked against the report text

paragraphs.controlling_idea: For an integrator 'single platform' does not mean one API: Adyen documents several API families with their own hosts and version counters and no call that returns a payment, so the claim is about one place where changes are made, not one interface.

evidence.what: Adyen's OpenAPI repository and versioning page (n.d., accessed November 2026): separate Checkout, Management, Configuration, Transfers, Legal Entity Management and Terminal APIs, each with its own version in the URL; Checkout API v72 has 31 operations of which 3 are GET and none returns a payment by its reference. Owned by payment-api-design, payment-api-versioning, payment-state-machines and payment-webhooks-and-events.
evidence.shows: The integrator's experience has seams that the phrase does not suggest; the mechanism chapters own the detail.

transition_in.carries_over: What Adyen says about the platform.
transition_in.introduces: What an integrator actually touches.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The third layer has a price Adyen reports: it runs its own infrastructure in data centers, which is the main part of a capital expenditure of 5% of net revenue in 2025 and an expected 7% in 2026.

evidence.what: Design to Duty part 1 (28 July 2021; evidence age 5 years): 'We manage our own infrastructure in several data centers around the world'; 'The reasons we are not deploying to the cloud are part historical, part legal, and part technical.' Adyen Annual Report 2025 (signed 5 March 2026; audited): 'CapEx was €116.8 million and 5% of net revenues for the full year. The majority of our CapEx is related to our data centers'. H1 2026 results release (13 August 2026): 'We are proactively pulling investment from 2027 into H2 2026 to secure compute and storage availability ... approximately 7% of net revenue this year.' H2 2023 release: capital expenditure was 7% of net revenue in 2022. Documentation (n.d., accessed November 2026): five live regions EU, US, AU, NEA, IN.
evidence.shows: Own hosting is documented across 2021, 2025 and 2026 and is a cost paid ahead of volume.

evidence.what: INFERENCE block: 'single platform' is an operating claim (one code base and one place to change), not an interface claim; its cost is fixed and paid before the volume arrives.
evidence.shows: The author's reading, labeled.

transition_in.carries_over: The platform as an operating claim.
transition_in.introduces: The infrastructure layer under it, and what it costs.

sections.heading: One Bank, Three Jurisdictions, and What the License Allows
sections.controlling_idea: Adyen is one Dutch credit institution with a US and a UK branch; the license lets it acquire, hold funds and pay out ahead of settlement on its own balance sheet, and Adyen discloses that it does not reach everywhere.

advances_thesis.how: Shows the second layer of the bet, what it buys in documented behavior, and the first of the edges Adyen itself reports.

transition_in.carries_over: The second layer of the bet, the licenses.
transition_in.introduces: Their legal form, their documented uses and their limits.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Legally Adyen is one credit institution supervised by the Dutch central bank, passported across the European Economic Area, with a federal branch in the United States and a branch in the United Kingdom, plus narrower local licenses elsewhere.

evidence.what: https://www.adyen.com/licenses/emea (n.d., accessed November 2026): 'Adyen N.V. is authorised as a credit Institution under the supervision of Dutch Central Bank'; 'authorised as an overseas branch of an EEA credit institution in the UK with a Part 4A permission'. https://www.adyen.com/licenses/united-states: 'a federal Branch of Adyen, N.V., licensed by the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and the Federal Reserve Board of Governors'. H1 2026 letter: 'a Category II payments license from the Central Bank of the UAE'. Singapore Major Payment Institution; Japan registration as merchant acquirer.
evidence.shows: One bank reused through branches, with payment licenses where a branch is not the route.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adyen says the licenses exist so that it does not depend on partner banks and has direct access to payment networks and control over funds, and the balance sheet shows the funds: €12.4 billion of cash at mid-2026, most of it merchants' money in transit, earning finance income.

evidence.what: Adyen Annual Report 2025 (signed 5 March 2026; audited): 'the speed and autonomy that come from not relying on external parties for regulatory compliance'. Adyen H1 2026 Shareholder Letter and interim statements (13 August 2026; unaudited): 'Our own licensed infrastructure grants direct access to payment networks, giving us control over funds'; 'We ended the half with €12.4 billion of total cash. The majority of that number represents balances moving through our system on behalf of our merchants'; finance income of €143.2 million 'generated primarily from our balances at central and commercial banks'. Annual Report 2025 income statement: finance income €267.6 million (2024: €349.8 million).
evidence.shows: The stated purpose and its trace in the accounts; finance income is separate from net revenue.

transition_in.introduces: What Adyen says it is for, and where it shows in the accounts.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The use an integrator sees most directly is the payout: under Sales day payout Adyen pays a day's sales after a fixed delay whether or not the card networks have paid Adyen, for up to 30 days, while its annual report calls paying after receipt the default.

evidence.what: Sales Day Payout Terms of Service (last update 17 June 2024): Adyen will 'initiate payout of the Net Captured Volume to Merchant on the Payout Day, irrespective of whether the funds are actually received by Adyen from the Acquirer or Scheme Owner'. Documentation (n.d., accessed November 2026): 'Prefinancing is capped at 30 days.' Adyen Annual Report 2025 (signed 5 March 2026; audited), risk section: 'In the default setup, Adyen follows a pass-through model, paying out to merchants only after funds have been received from the payment method. Liquidity mismatches can arise only when deviating from this default, primarily through pre-financing in accelerated payout schedules.'
evidence.shows: Pre-financing is documented for Adyen (ruling 18); the two documents describe the default differently, which the article reports without resolving.

transition_in.introduces: The documented behavior that control makes possible: paying out ahead of settlement.

sections.heading: The Figures, With Their Definitions
sections.controlling_idea: Processed volume, net revenue, take rate and EBITDA margin measure different things, moved differently in 2025, and can be explained from Adyen's own reporting; the margin's link to the platform is Adyen's attribution.

advances_thesis.how: Gives the audited figures with definitions and works the year in which they diverged.

transition_in.carries_over: The acquisitions, which change headcount, margin guidance and capital spending in 2026.
transition_in.introduces: The figures those changes show up in, defined before they are read.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Four measures carry Adyen's reporting: processed volume (the value handled), net revenue (what Adyen keeps after passing on interchange and scheme fees), take rate (net revenue over volume, in basis points) and EBITDA margin (EBITDA over net revenue); a table gives them for 2023 to the third quarter of 2026.

evidence.what: Metric | 2023 | 2024 | 2025 | H1 2026 | Q3 2026: processed volume €970.1B, €1,285.9B, €1,394.3B, €803.8B, €451.1B; net revenue €1,626.1M, €1,996.1M, €2,364.2M, €1,302.9M, €738.1M; EBITDA margin 46%, 50%, 53%, 49%, not reported; take rate n/a, 15.5 bps, 17.0 bps, 16.2 bps, not given; in-person volume €159.9B, €232.7B, €310.9B, €175.7B, not given.
evidence.shows: One place for the figures, with audited and unaudited periods marked.

evidence.what: Adyen Annual Report 2025 (signed 5 March 2026; audited), note 2.2 and revenue note: net revenue is a non-IFRS measure, net non-interest revenue (non-interest revenue less 'costs incurred from financial institutions' and costs of goods sold) plus net interest income; €2,351.6 million plus €12.6 million in 2025. Processed volume is not defined in one sentence in the report.
evidence.shows: The definitions come from the audited notes; the missing definition is stated.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: In 2025 volume grew 8% and net revenue 18% because a single large-volume customer, unnamed, processed less: excluding it volume grew 21%, the take rate rose from 15.5 to 17.0 basis points through merchant mix, and in the first half of 2026 it fell back to 16.2 through volume tiering.

evidence.what: H2 2025 release (12 February 2026): 'Processed volume was €1,394.3 billion, up 21% excluding a single large-volume customer, or 8% YoY including this customer.' Adyen Annual Report 2025 (signed 5 March 2026; audited): 'Full-year take rate for 2025 was 17.0 bps, up from 15.5 bps in 2024. This increase was driven by changes in the overall merchant mix.' Adyen H1 2026 Shareholder Letter and interim statements (13 August 2026; unaudited): 'Take rate landed at 16.2 bps, reflecting expected volume tiering'. Adyen Q3 2026 Business Update (28 October 2026; unaudited): 'Adyen's tiered pricing structure incentivizes our customers to bring more volume to our platform.' Pricing page (n.d., accessed November 2026): 'a fixed processing fee + a fee determined by the payment method', Interchange++.
evidence.shows: Adyen's own explanation is mix and tiers, not a price increase (AC-2).

transition_in.introduces: A year in which the measures moved apart, worked from them.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The revenue comes from three pillars and is spread across large customers: the top ten merchants were 11% of 2025 revenue, none above 10%, and Adyen's own risk section says large merchants typically use several providers.

evidence.what: Adyen Annual Report 2025 (signed 5 March 2026; audited): pillars Digital €1,334.9 million, Unified Commerce €765.4 million, Platforms €263.8 million; 'Adyen's top 10 merchants represent 11% of revenue (2024: 12%)'; 'Large enterprise merchants typically work with multiple payment service providers to mitigate their own single-point-of-failure risk. As a result, these customers may terminate contracts or shift volume elsewhere'. Adyen H1 2026 Shareholder Letter and interim statements (13 August 2026; unaudited): 'Our typical share of wallet increases from under 20% in years 3–7 to over 40% after year 12'.
evidence.shows: Even Adyen's customers do not treat one platform as the only one; Adyen reports it as a risk and as a growth path (AC-3).

transition_in.introduces: Whose volume it is.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Adyen attributes its margin to the single platform; the same documents show the margin following hiring and investment, with the 2026 expectation cut to 50% and the medium-term objective withdrawn on 28 October 2026.

evidence.what: Adyen H1 2026 Shareholder Letter and interim statements (13 August 2026; unaudited): EBITDA margin 49% (50% excluding €6.0 million of transaction costs), 'demonstrating the underlying operational efficiency inherent to our single-platform architecture as we scale'. Investor Day release (11 November 2025): 'above 55% by 2028'. Adyen Q3 2026 Business Update (28 October 2026; unaudited): 'we now expect EBITDA margin of 50% in 2026. To retain flexibility, we are discontinuing our medium-term EBITDA objective'; capital expenditure 7% of net revenue; 5,596 FTE including 399 from the acquisitions.
evidence.shows: The attribution is Adyen's; the guidance change shows the margin is also a choice about investment.

evidence.what: INFERENCE block: a margin of 53% is evidence that the model is profitable at Adyen's scale, not that the architecture causes it; 2023 and 2026 both show it moving with headcount. Volume is not revenue: about €1 of net revenue for every €590 processed in 2025 (author's arithmetic).
evidence.shows: Labels the causal reading as the author's.

sections.heading: The Engineering Record, and How Old It Is
sections.controlling_idea: Adyen has published few engineering accounts; the architecture series dates from 2018 to 2021, and newer posts confirm scale and own hosting without describing topology.

advances_thesis.how: Sets out what is documented about internals with its age, so that the transfer table rests on dated evidence.

transition_in.carries_over: Figures that are current and audited.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Of the hundreds of pages on Adyen's knowledge hub only a few dozen are engineering posts, the ones that describe architecture are from 2018 to 2021, and the newer ones cover databases, streaming and one incident.

evidence.what: Adyen knowledge hub, by date: 'From 0 to $100 billion' (3 January 2018), 'Design to Duty' parts 1 and 2 (28 July and 23 August 2021), a five-part PostgreSQL partitioning series (2023 to 2025), the DDoS incident update (22 April 2025) and its follow-up (31 October 2025), 'We built Architect for humans' (August 2026). Not found: topology, failover design, a deploy count comparable to Stripe's (the Infrastructure page states weekly releases of the core system), a postmortem.
evidence.shows: The base for every statement about internals is small and mostly old.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The 2021 account describes a stateless acceptance layer that favors uptime and an accounting system that favors consistency, fed through a local database queue, where records can be added only through templates proven to sum to zero.

evidence.what: Design to Duty part 2 (23 August 2021; evidence age 5 years): 'for the accounting systems we don't mind if they are down for a little bit as long as we can guarantee their reliability and consistency'; 'The only way to add new records to the accounting system is by means of templates'; 'These templates are mathematically verified'; 'if at any time, we sum up all the records in the accounting system, the result will always be 0'. Owned by payment-ledgers and payment-reliability-and-availability.
evidence.shows: The practice a builder can take is stated here; it is five years old and may describe a replaced system.

transition_in.introduces: Its most useful item: the 2021 design of the edge and the books.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: The same posts describe PostgreSQL clusters sharded round-robin at a stated cost, a Java monorepo, and development on one main line with features switched on one by one; no deployment frequency for the platform is public.

Part 1 (2021): 'a single platform, in a single repository (monorepo), almost exclusively written in Java'. 'From 0 to $100 billion' (2018; evidence age 8 years): 'everybody develops on the main line'; 'we toggle features one-by-one on production, and then canary them'. Architect post (August 2026): 'Our monorepo alone runs to hundreds of thousands of files, and it's far from the only one.' Owned by payment-data-stores-and-consistency and payment-safe-change.

transition_in.introduces: The storage under them and the way changes reach production.

paragraphs.controlling_idea: Sources from 2025 and 2026 confirm the scale and the cost of running your own edge: about 3,000 live services on tens of thousands of hosts in tens of data centers, and one attack in April 2025 that Adyen answered partly by adding outside mitigation providers.

evidence.what: Architect post (August 2026): 'around 3,000 live services and the ~470,000 calls between them'; 'tens of thousands of hosts spread across tens of data centres'. evidence.what: INFERENCE block: 'single platform' is not a single process; the in-house rule bends where a specialist is cheaper than the risk; the public picture of the internals is a 2021 snapshot plus a few later measurements.

sections.heading: What Transfers to a Builder, and What Does Not
sections.controlling_idea: Three practices in Adyen's record can be adopted at any size and three assets cannot be copied; Adyen's own customers show the limit of relying on one platform.

conclusion.heading: What to Take Away
conclusion.synthesis: Read together, the history, the bet, the edges and the figures say something no section says alone: Adyen's single platform is the result of an order of construction that took from 2006 to 2023 and is priced in its accounts, and the same company that built it is the one that marks its limits and, in 2026, went outside it. The phrase is accurate with a scope and a date, and misleading without them.
conclusion.so_what: A customer asks of each Adyen product whether it runs on the platform or was bought, and what is shared; a builder takes the accounting discipline and the one-place-for-change rule and does not mistake a bank, a data-center footprint or a margin for an architecture pattern.

callback.to: The retailer architect's sentence from the opening: 'Adyen builds everything itself on one platform, so whatever we buy from them is one integration with one set of reports.'
callback.how: The reader can now give it a scope (payments, acquiring, terminals, banking products) and a date (on the author's reading, true of everything Adyen sold until 30 June 2026), and name the two products it no longer covers.

takeaway.content: For every Adyen product you use or plan to use, write down whether it runs on the platform Adyen built or was bought in 2026, which entity acquires and holds funds in each country, which payout model applies, and the date and source of each answer; ask Adyen for what the public record does not say.

hand_off.carries_over: The two records as the cases leave them: Stripe, the interface first and the regulated layer assembled afterward as a non-bank; Adyen, the license and platform first and adjacent software bought in 2026; each with its own list of what is not public.
hand_off.introduces: The two set side by side on the same rows, with the 'Where They Differ' tables of Parts I to VIII gathered under them and sorted by the kind of evidence behind each difference.

Depends on context: whether 'one platform' means one integration depends on which products you buy and when; whether Adyen acquires and pre-finances for you depends on the country and the payout model; whether its practices suit you depends on what you build, since the practices scale down and the assets do not.

Adyen's agent-payment products, stablecoin clause and instant-payment schemes.
Share price, valuation and analyst opinion; the 2023 Investor Day targets and the August 2023 share-price fall, which were not fetched.

Any description of Adyen's topology, failover design or hardware security modules beyond what Adyen states (six named regions, failover by load balancers, weekly releases of the core system): not public, and not inferred here.

open_questions: The journal entry says Adyen was founded 'with a European acquiring license'. Adyen's history page lists the license among the steps of 2006 to 2012 without a year; the article says so and does not date the license to 2006.

The journal entry calls Talon.One and Orb Adyen's 'first two acquisitions'. No Adyen document read says so; Adyen's history page lists no earlier acquisition. The article says 'no earlier acquisition appears in Adyen's own history'.
The annual report describes pass-through payout as 'the default setup' while the documentation presents Sales day payout as the standard model; the article reports both and does not resolve them.
'Full-stack' is not defined at the point where the 84% is reported; the article labels its reading as inference.

decision_log.decision: Section order follows the order the journal entry's AC-4 expects (history, bet, licenses, in-person, platforms, acquisitions, figures, engineering, transfers, evidence stops).
rejected: Figures directly after the history, as in ORDERED's cases: the 2026 guidance change cannot be read before the acquisitions.
